# Construction and Destruction Order
<!-- Slide 43 -->

## Who Is Built First? {.smaller}

- A Student has a Person part and a Transcript member. Which is built first, and which is destroyed first?

::: notes
Slides 44–49

Students know two rules from 11.01, members before the body and destruction in reverse, and one from Topic 4, the base before the members. This topic puts them together.
:::

<!-- Slide 44 -->

---

## Predict the Output

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="60%"}
::: {style="font-size: 50%;"}
~~~cpp
class Person {
public:
    Person() { cout << "Person built" << endl; }
    ~Person() { cout << "Person destroyed" << endl; }
};

class Transcript {
public:
    Transcript() { cout << "Transcript built" << endl; }
    ~Transcript() { cout << "Transcript destroyed" << endl; }
};

class Student : public Person {
private:
    Transcript record;

public:
    Student() { cout << "Student body" << endl; }
    ~Student() { cout << "~Student body" << endl; }
};

int main() {
    Student ava;
    cout << "--- end of main ---" << endl;
    return 0;
}
~~~
:::
:::

::: {.column width="40%"}
. . .

~~~
Person built
Transcript built
Student body
--- end of main ---
~Student body
Transcript destroyed
Person destroyed
~~~
:::

::::

::: notes
Have students write all seven lines before revealing them.

Full program: cpp/order.cpp
:::

<!-- Slide 45 -->

---

## The Rule

| Building | Destroying |
|---|---|
| 1. The base class part | 1. The derived destructor body |
| 2. Members, in declaration order | 2. Members, in reverse declaration order |
| 3. The derived constructor body | 3. The base class part |

- Destruction is construction run backward.

::: notes
This is 11.01's member rule with the base class added at the front of building and at the end of destroying.
:::

<!-- Slide 46 -->

---

## Why Reverse?

- `~Student` may still use its Person part, for example to call `getName()` in a goodbye message.
- If the Person part went first, `~Student` would read a dead object, like the dangling pointer in 11.01.
- Last built, first destroyed: every part outlives everything built on top of it.

::: notes
The same reasoning explains members: Student's destructor body may still use record, so record is destroyed after the body runs.
:::

<!-- Slide 47 -->

---

## Three Levels

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="60%"}
::: {style="font-size: 50%;"}
~~~cpp
class Person {
public:
    Person() { cout << "Person" << endl; }
    ~Person() { cout << "~Person" << endl; }
};

class Student : public Person {
public:
    Student() { cout << "Student" << endl; }
    ~Student() { cout << "~Student" << endl; }
};

class GradStudent : public Student {
public:
    GradStudent() { cout << "GradStudent" << endl; }
    ~GradStudent() { cout << "~GradStudent" << endl; }
};

int main() {
    GradStudent ava;
    cout << "--- end of main ---" << endl;
    return 0;
}
~~~
:::
:::

::: {.column width="40%"}
. . .

~~~
Person
Student
GradStudent
--- end of main ---
~GradStudent
~Student
~Person
~~~
:::

::::

::: notes
Ask students to predict before revealing. The rule repeats at every level: GradStudent's base part is a Student, whose base part is a Person, so the oldest ancestor is built first and destroyed last.

Full program: cpp/three_levels.cpp
:::

<!-- Slide 48 -->

---

## Summary

- Built: base part, then members in declaration order, then the body.
- Destroyed: in exactly the reverse order, so every part outlives what was built on top of it.

::: notes

:::
